name: Heberprot-P

lead: Heberprot-P is an injectable formulation of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (EGF), made by Cuba's Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology and marketed by Heber Biotec. It is used for advanced diabetic foot ulcers, and it comes up in discussions of EGF for skin healing and renewal.

EGF stimulates skin cell growth. In patients with ulcers it is injected into and around the wound base to promote granulation tissue and faster wound closure. Human reports are mostly small series plus one registered phase 3 trial, all in ulcers; no studies of cosmetic use were found.

paras: It is given by clinicians into and around the wound as a medical treatment. It is not used as a cosmetic product.
It is a medical product given by clinicians, and per Wikipedia it was not approved in the US as of 2016. Safety information in the sources reviewed is limited.

angle.text: Heberprot-P is a Cuban injectable EGF used for diabetic foot ulcers, where it stimulates cell growth for faster wound closure, and it comes up in discussions of EGF for skin healing. Wound-healing evidence is small-scale and covers ulcers.

lead: Heberprot-P is an injectable formulation of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (rhEGF, nepidermin) developed by Cuba's Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (CIBG) and marketed by Heber Biotec. It is given into and around the base and edges of advanced diabetic foot ulcers to stimulate granulation tissue and wound closure.[1][2]

Epidermal growth factor is a signalling protein that prompts skin cells to divide and migrate, and EGF-containing serums and regenerative skin products are discussed in appearance circles for that reason. Heberprot-P is the prescription, injected, wound-healing form of the molecule; it is not a cosmetic product, and no studies of it for cosmetic outcomes were found.[2] Its relevance to looks is therefore through the broader interest in growth factors for skin repair and regeneration.

Published clinical experience consists mainly of small series from Cuba, Turkey and elsewhere reporting granulation and closure of chronic ulcers, with one registered phase 3 placebo-controlled trial of 304 participants.[3][4][5][2] Wikipedia reports it was marketed in 23 countries as of 2016 and is unavailable in the United States.[2]
infobox: 2006; added to national basic medicines list 2007[1]
Registered in about 15 other countries, over 100,000 patients treated (2013 review)[1]

paras: Epidermal growth factor was discovered by Stanley Cohen, working with Rita Levi-Montalcini at Washington University in St. Louis during research on nerve growth factor; the two shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. [6] EGF binds the EGF receptor on the cell surface with high affinity, causing the receptor to pair up and activate its tyrosine kinase, which signals onward to DNA synthesis and cell proliferation. [6] Because of this effect on skin cell division and migration, EGF is a common name in regenerative skincare, although cosmetic uses lie outside Heberprot-P's labelled use. [6]

Nepidermin uses the 53-amino-acid human EGF sequence and is produced by inserting that sequence into yeast; its molecular formula is C270H401N73O83S7, with a molar mass of about 6,222 g/mol. Wikipedia describes it as the first EGF receptor agonist to be marketed, with intralesional and topical routes.[2]

A 2013 MEDICC Review article explains the rationale: diabetic tissue has lower growth-factor concentrations, particularly EGF, which impairs healing, and injecting EGF deep into the wound base and margins is said to produce a stronger granulation response than surface application. The same review says the injected growth factor may associate with extracellular matrix proteins, enhancing cell proliferation and migration.[1]

In a Cuban study of biopsies from 10 responding patients before and after two weeks of treatment, expression of genes linked to proliferation, angiogenesis and matrix formation (including PDGFB, ANGPT1 and COL1A1) rose, while inflammation and oxidative-stress genes (NFKB1, TNFA, IL1A) fell.[7]

Heberprot-P is used for deep diabetic foot ulcers, including ischemic ones, with the aim of promoting granulation and closure and reducing amputation risk [1]. Wikipedia reports sale in 23 countries as of 2016 and unavailability in the United States.

Cuba registered the product in 2006 and added it to its national basic medicines list in 2007, and it has since been registered in about 15 other countries and used in more than 100,000 patients, according to a 2013 review from Cuban authors.[1] Wikipedia lists the brand names Heberprot-P, Easyef, Genesoft, Kang He Su and Regen-D for rhEGF products, which are marketed for diabetic foot ulcers, wounds and, in Asia, alopecia.[2]

Pilot series with complete closure. A pilot study in 20 diabetic patients with full-thickness ulcers over 4 weeks old (mean size 16.3 cm2) gave intralesional injections three times a week until healed: all showed full granulation in about 24 days, 17 (85 percent) closed completely in about 44 days, none needed amputation and one relapsed; common adverse events were tremors, chills, pain and odour at the site and local infection.[3] A similar 17-patient study reported full granulation in all, closure in 16 (94.1 percent) in about 53 days, and one relapse at one year.[4]

Turkish reports. In a 58-patient observational study at Duzce State Hospital, wound healing with granulation was reported in 93.1 percent, amputation in two patients (3.4 percent), and tremor and syncope as the most common adverse events.[8] A retrospective comparison of 29 treated patients against 22 controls found shorter treatment times and higher healing rates with Heberprot-P, with a lower amputation rate that did not reach statistical significance.[9] A series of 12 limb-threatening ischemic lesions in 11 patients who had failed revascularization, hyperbaric oxygen and negative pressure therapy reported 10 lesions healed and two amputations, with the authors noting the high cost of the product.[10] A 2025 three-group study of 31 patients found re-epithelialisation in about 70 days with Heberprot-P (alone or with adipose-derived stromal vascular fraction) versus about 188 days with conventional care.[11]

Registered trials. A phase 3 placebo-controlled trial of 304 participants (NCT02554851) was registered in 2017 with unknown status,[5] and a 50-patient trial at the Dasman Diabetes Institute in Kuwait has been completed.[12] A 2022 zebrafish study compared it with another EGF product.[13] Most published human reports are small and uncontrolled.

Adverse events reported in the series above include tremors, chills, pain, burning and odour at the injection site, local infection and, in one series, syncope.[3][4][8] Registered trials list efficacy and safety as outcomes.[5][12] Epidermal growth factor stimulates cell proliferation, and the cited publications are about diabetic foot ulcers rather than cosmetic or long-term use.

Heberprot-P is a product of Cuba's biotechnology sector, and Wikipedia reports that its path to the US has been stalled: preparations for phase 3 trials aimed at FDA approval began in 2015, and as of 2023 developments in US-Cuba relations have blocked importing the drug.[2] Wikipedia also notes that potency varies by expression system and that bioassay standardisation is still developing.[2]

Wikipedia calls nepidermin the first EGF receptor agonist to be marketed and classes it as a cicatrizant, a drug that promotes wound healing through scar formation. [2] Heber Biotech has marketed Heberprot-P since 2006, and other rhEGF products are sold in Vietnam, the Philippines, Thailand and China; Easyef from Korea is a spray and Regen-D from Bharat Biotech in India is a gel approved in India and Thailand. [2] Wikipedia notes that rhEGF products are marketed for alopecia as well as wounds, and lists nepidermin among alopecia treatments, without giving further detail. [2] The epidermal growth factor page states that tentative evidence suggests improved wound healing with rhEGF and that safety has been poorly studied. [6]
